speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RIGHT OP MEMBER TO REVISE REMARKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it becomes my unfortunate duty to deal with a matter affecting the privileges of the house. My attention was directed to the fact that during the course of a speech in the house the night before last the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said:
I am not in favour of an election this year.
That remark does not appear in Hansard, and it now transpires that the words were taken down by the Hansard reporter and struck out of the report by the hon. gentleman. I hold the original manuscript in my
Civil Service Committee

hand. Though as much care as can be exercised is taken in connection with these matters I think it well to direct attention to the fact that the privileges extended to members do not permit of the elimination from their remarks of statements of this kind.

subtopic: RIGHT OP MEMBER TO REVISE REMARKS
speechtext: I quite agree with the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, but I could quote an instance where one of his ministers struck out a passage from one of his speeches last year which made it appear exactly opposite to what he had said. Since then, however, he has taken a flight to Egypt.

subtopic: RIGHT OP MEMBER TO REVISE REMARKS
speechtext: I have had occasion before this to believe that members have struck out portions of their speeches. We shall have to be more watchful in future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RIGHT OP MEMBER TO REVISE REMARKS
speechtext: I believe the rule has been that grammatical errors and defects of that sort are corrected. In one case I made some inquiries when it was brought to my attention that substantial changes had been made in a speech; the matter was brought to the attention of the house, and the Hansard authorities were advised that it was not competent for anyone to change the sense of a speech. There may be errors in transcription or there may be errors made in taking down the remarks of the speaker because of noise in the chamber. Those are matters with which members may be expected to deal quite properly. I recall in my own case that on one occasion there was a noise in the chamber and Hansard sent for me saying that because of the noise they had not been able to take down what had been said, and wanting to know if I could assist them. I gave them my notes, such as they were-they were not very helpful-and I am bound to say that the report was not entirely intelligent. In this case, however, the words were heard and transcribed, but they have been struck out by the hon. gentleman who used them. It becomes somewhat important for the reason that a few moments previously the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) had been speaking of the necessity for an early appeal to the country. Then one of the distinguished members opposite, who frequently speaks for the Liberal party, said he was not in favour of an election this year, and though Hansard took down these words they were struck out by the hon. member.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RIGHT OP MEMBER TO REVISE REMARKS
speechtext:
I think I heard the remark that was made by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I do not know how much of the text he removed, but the remark 
about not being in favour of an election this year was associated with a further remark, provided that the present leader of the government was not retained as leader. If the hon. member for Temiscouata struck that out he evidently felt .that he did not wish to reflect upon the present Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RIGHT OP MEMBER TO REVISE REMARKS
speechtext:
No, he left that in. The very courteous observation made by the right hon. gentleman makes it possible for me to read the whole sentence as it was taken down by the reporter and transcribed into typewriting. It was as follows:
I am not in favour of an election this year; we can wait another year, provided that the Conservative party .and the government select another leader to devise new measures and carry on for another year.
What appears, as amended in the handwriting of the hon. member, is this: first, there is the deletion of the words "I am not in favour of an election this year." Then the following words appear:
We might wait another year for an election -provided that the Conservative party and the government select another leader-and try the administration for a year longer under that new leadership.
The last twelve words are in the handwriting of the hon. member, so he did not remove that portion of his observations.

subtopic: RIGHT OP MEMBER TO REVISE REMARKS
speechtext: I am glad the right hon. gentleman has taken notice of that fact.

He said:	Mr. Speaker, in moving this

Supply-Public Works-Quebec
outside Canada and not in the empire, has the government any control over the use of such material?

What is the basis on which
the government acquires these buildings?

These armouries are constructed by local associations, in each case, in the city where the building is located. They provide the capital and the government undertakes to pay by instalments, over a period of years, an equal amount in each year covering the cost of construction. The building then becomes the property of the dominion.

I object to that form of
contract being entered into by the government with any private corporation. When public buildings are to be erected the government can better afford to put them up than any private organization. In the first place, an armoury is a public building and should be owned by the government; and secondly, when a private organization contracts to erect such a building, it has to go on the public market to obtain funds and is compelled to pay much higher interest than would be paid if the government itself were directly responsible for the undertaking. There must be a difference of one and a half or two per cent in the cost. The government assumes liability to purchase the building over a term of years, and it simply means that it is compelled to pay a larger sum than it would pay if it were responsible for financing the construction. Why does the government allow a private organization to become responsible for the erection of such buildings, when the government is ultimately responsible for them?

It is a practice
that has been followed by governments for some considerable time. There is something to be said in favour of my hon. friend's contention, but we must bear in mind that these public works are constructed out of revenue. We do not borrow, except in very few instances, money for the construction of public buildings. These buildings are an expense, and to take the cost out of any one year's revenue

would be a very severe charge indeed. Therefore, instead of the government borrowing the money, spreading it over a period of years, it adopts this plan of allowing the local association to construct the building. The association takes the initiative in these matters. They have an interest in it, and it is from the local standpoint that the undertaking is initiated; it is not done on the initiative of the government. From the time the building is completed however it is the property of the government; it is taken over from the contractor. It is under the control of the government and is used by the Department of National Defence.
If it were not for the government's guarantee the private corporation would not be able to finance construction?
It is doubtful whether they would be able to finance it if there were not the undertaking to pay by instalment.
The government in any case has the responsibility of paying for the buildings; it is liable. Does the government supervise the awarding of the contracts for these buildings?

The expenditures have to meet with the approval of the government under the terms of an agreement made with the association. It must be remembered that these are buildings which, in the natural course of events, should be constructed by the government. They are not buildings that should be constructed by any private corporation. The architect is appointed by the association and the government exercises very close supervision over expenditures, and if there is anything outside the scope of the standard agreement which has been developed and perfected over a period of years the expenditure is not approved and the association must stand the expense themselves. There are some instances in which associations do expend amounts in addition to those approved of.
In connection with this particular undertaking, will the contracts be awarded by tender?

I cannot say
whether in every instance they have been advertised, but I know of no instance in which there has not been competition. I have in mind one building in connection with which tenders were invited from nine or ten different people, although in that particular case there was no public advertisement.

The reason why I am asking this question must I am sure be obvious to the minister. I have in mind a certain city where they contemplate the construction of an armoury along -the same lines as the undertaking we are discussing at the moment. It has come to my knowledge that this particular construction will be awarded by private tender. A private corporation is being created to undertake the work, and the only basis on which the money will be loaned is the intention of the government to lease the building over a period of twenty years. I have a strong objection to the government guaranteeing any private corporation in the construction of public buildings, for the maintenance of which -the government becomes responsible, though the building remains under the ownership of a private organization for a period of years. Surely the government is strong enough to erect these buildings in whatever part of the country they are required. Coming back to the city I have in mind, a private corporation is being created there to construct an armoury. The government takes a lease of the building for twenty years. At the end of these twenty years the building will have been completely paid for and will then revert to the ownership of the government; but in the meantime the private contractor will receive from twenty to forty thousand dollars more than if the work were advertised and done by public tender. That is where my objection comes in to the construction of these buildings. I believe that in order to avoid anything savouring of favouritism or overcharging in the construction of buildings the only fair thing to do is for the government -to own these buildings themselves completely, advertising by way of public tender, and giving every contractor an opportunity of tendering. I should like to get from the minister an understanding that if any more of these buildings are constructed the government itself, whether through the Department of Public Works or the Department of National Defence, will be responsible for letting the tenders and giving every contractor a chance to tender.

I wish to associate myself to some extent with the criticism of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) regarding the purchase-rental method of constructing public buildings of any kind. If such a building is necessary the government should assume the responsibility and place before the house an estimate for such construction. I believe the purchase rental method is an evasion of the rights of this
parliament; the matter is brought before the government and a contract entered into without parliament being consulted. The government enters into obligations and then comes to the House of Commons and says:	We
have these obligations and it is now your duty to pass these amounts. The minister has explained how this has been brought about. An association is formed and I think the minister will agree with me that it is purely a paper organization; it is based entirely on the strength of the contract that they can enter into with the government. The question of calling for tenders is technically left with the organization; they may call for tenders or they may not. The government may require the calling of tenders and as a matter of fact usually they do, but after all, the government have entered into a contract with a paper organization and are to all intents and purposes giving them great freedom in the manner in which they conduct their business.
If we are to have armouries in Canada- and I for one believe we must have them-[DOT] we should carry out the armoury business in an open and aboveboard manner, place the estimates for such construction before the house, let the house consider whether such construction is advisable or not and if we cannot get public opinion as expressed in the House of Commons to support such measures, then I do not think the particular armoury in question should be erected. In the past the reason this method was adopted was due to fear on the part of some members of the government of the day that they could not secure the support of the house for the construction of armouries. I for one believe that time has passed, but I do not think that method should ever have been adopted, and I suggest to the government that if they wish to construct armouries in future, they should lay their plans before the house and let us consider what armouries we should , have in Canada.

I am afraid there
is some misconception in this matter; these are simply regimental armouries built for one regiment. The association mentioned is a regimental one and in no case are the plans of the association approved by the Department of Public Works before the Department of National Defence have passed on and approved them. Moreover, the first allotment on the first contract made with either the Department of National Defence or the Department of Public Works is always submitted to the House of Commons when the

Supply-Public Works-Quebec
first instalment is voted in advance of construction. The only armouries of the kind that have been built in the past are, as I said before, regimental armouries for one regiment or brigade. All other armouries affecting other arms of the service or for more than one regiment in one city are always built by the Department of Public Works.
The hon. member has completely evaded the real issue at stake.
I was not replying to the hon. member.

I am trying to point out
that the question has nothing to do with the purpose for which the building is being constructed. The point is whether the erection of public buildings is to be turned over to private corporations. If public buildings are to be erected, the proper body to control their erection is parliament; parliament should have control over the money it is voting and over the building once it is erected. I did not even raise the question of armouries or oppose their construction; I am raising an entirely different point. I object to parliament being asked to vote money to a private organization. If parliament is responsible for the erection of a public building, it should control the money and the building itself. Will the minister say that in future no such plans will be approved by the government, but that parliament will assume all responsibility in connection with the erection of such buildings?
This practice, as I have said, is not new. I think it originated in 1925 in connection with the construction of an armoury in the city of Montreal.
Was it not Regina?
Westmount.

I think the
Montreal armoury preceded the Regina one. The former Deputy Minister of National Defence understands the situation very well and the reason these buildings have been constructed as they have. Let me say to the hon. member for North Winnipeg that these buildings are from the time of completion of construction taken over by and under the control of the government, and then handed to the regiment that occupies them in the usual way that military buildings are occupied. I point out to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard that the matter must
[Sir Eugene Fiset.l
come to parliament for approval of the first item in the estimates and then the whole question is up for discussion. If parliament rejects the item in the estimates, the matter cannot proceed; it is all subject to the approval of parliament.

Is any contract entered
into before the first estimate is approved?

You cannot enter into a contract before you have a vote of parliament for the amount required. We never enter into a contract until the matter is discussed in parliament and the vote passed. It is on the strength of that vote that the agreement is made with the association.

The minister says that
after the completion of the contract, the government have full control of the building. I understand that legally the building remains in the possession of the building company for a period of years. I believe a limited liability company is formed and this company have officers and hold meetings, and continue to do so for a period of years. The building, while it may be actually in the possession of the government, is technically in possession of the building company.
Until it is paid for.
Yes.

It is my
understanding-and I would ask to be corrected by the minister if I am wrong!-when the contract is completed and the armoury is taken over by the government, title is thereupon vested in the government, and instead of the government having technical it has legal possession from the time of completion of the armoury.

As I understand the
matter, title is not in the government; it is in the association, but it is under an instalment purchase agreement whereby possession is in the government, so that nothing but the bare title remains in the association and at the end of twenty years, or whatever the term may be, the building automatically comes under the control of the government in the sense not only of possession but of title. The principal objection I have seen to this method-and as a former minister I have at least on one occasion presented to the house a similar estimate-is whether we could get money at the same rate of interest in this way as if the money were borrowed directly. There is a great deal to be said

Supply-Public Works-Quebec
for what hon. members on this side have stated, and probably the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of National Defence will agree. I know I sat in this chamber one night in 1928 or 1929 and heard the present leader of the government absolutely rave, if I may use the word without offence, with regard to a similar proposition in Regina, but it seems that the situation is different now that the right hon. .gentleman is himself leader of a government. The principal objection is the question of interest, but outside of that I do not think there is any question but that the government's interests are protected in every particular.
May I say further, in regard to the Victoria Rifles armoury building, which is the first item in vote 97, that if ever there was a case of merit it seems to me this was a genuine case. For many years that regiment supplied their own armoury premises, which they owned themselves, and of which they gave the government the benefit of the use. I have forgotten whether the building finally went into disrepair or whether it was burned.

A tunnel was put
through.

Yes, and the premises
were rendered unfit for use. Then, and only then, this regiment came to the government and asked them to supply premises for them, and that is what this particular vote is for. With regard to the Westmount armouries, I understand that that was started in 1925. Will the minister tell me how many instalments are still due on that building.
The first payment on the Westmount armoury was made for the year 1926-27 and amounted to $12,624. We have made eight payments, so there are twelve payments yet to be made.
Has the minister any information as to the manner in which these associations raise the money for the erection of these buildings, and what rate of interest is charged?

I believe they
issue debentures, and so far as we are concerned the rate of interest is limited to five per cent.
Would the minister tell me whether under this method of erecting buildings the contractors are governed by the fair wage and eight hour day law passed in 1930?

The clauses regarding minimum wages and so on as laid down by the Department of Labour are sent
to these associations, who must embody them in their contracts. We see that this is done.
Has the minister received any requests for the construction of a post office at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, and if so is there any likelihood that it will be constructed in the near future.
I cannot recall any very recent request, but I should be surprised if at some time during the last few years we have not received a request for the construction of a post office there.
Would the minister be kind enough to secure this information?
Certainly; I shall find out when and by whom the last request was made.
Would the minister say whether any buildings used for other purposes are constructed and taken over by the government on the same principle.

I understand that in the past some buildings have been acquired in a similar way. My deputy informs me that the Daly building in Ottawa was purchased on the instalment plan as well as a certain building that we use for workshops. These building were not constructed on the same basis and then acquired, but were purchased from the owners on the instalment plan.

That is quite a different principle. The reason I asked that question was because I am of the opinion that there is something in the contention expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard that this is a sort of underhand way of building armouries in this country. There may be other reasons why it is done in this way but undoubtedly this is one of the main reasons.

In reply to my hon. friend I can assure him that there is nothing underhand about it. There can be nothing underhand when we come to this house and ask for approval of an estimate for this purpose. Just as much information is given in connection with this vote as is given in connection with any other.
Mr. HANB'URY: I should like to ask the minister whether the government would give sympathetic consideration to further construction under this plan.

It seems to me that my hon. friend's request cancels the suggestion made by the hon. member for North Winnipeg who asked me to give a pledge that this would not be done again.

I understand that my hon. friend suggests that I should give him a pledge that it will be done.
No, I ask for sympathetic consideration.

It would not be very sympathetic if we did not do it. Of course I cannot pledge the government as to what their policy will be in any particular case. They will have to be guided by what appears to be best in the circumstances as they are presented in each instance. There is precedence for this action; there is also some merit in it. I recognize the force of the objections to it, but in this case it has been adopted apparently with fairly satisfactory results to all concerned.

I presume the government are obligated to the amounts set out in the estimates, but I am raising the question in regard to future construction of a similar type. I am asking two things: First, if the department feels it necessary to construct armouries that they should construct them on their own responsibility; second, that if the government do not want to assume the responsibility for the erection of these buildings and think it a better policy to have private corporations undertake their construction, then I want the government to undertake to see that these buildings are constructed by public tender and put up in such a way as to ensure that the government will get the best possible results for the money for which they become responsible. I should like to have the minister's reply to those two suggestions.

The specifications are submitted to the Department of Public Works for revision and approval, and are also submitted for the approval of the Department of National Defence. I cannot give my hon. friend any undertaking that in no case will an armoury be constructed on any plan other than this or that all armouries will be constructed by the government. I can assure him that we will endeavour to see that reasonable competition is secured. Certainly we would not approve of the construction of a building at an extravagant cost. We have our own estimates, and I know of no case in which a contract has been awarded privately or as the result of only one tender. We would want to be satisfied that there was honest, real competition in connection with the awarding of the contract.

I should like to ask the minister for the particulars of the third item, amounting to $2,400, for the city of Toronto.

This is to provide for payment of the government's share of the following local improvements in the city of Toronto: sewer on Lombard street between Victoria and Church streets, $1,116.29; an asphalt pavement on Lombardi street between Victoria and Church streets, $1,249.97, or a total of $2,366.26, say $2,400 to cover contingencies. I just wish to bring to the attention of the committee certain anomalies respecting public buildings in the city of Ottawa, and certain public works. Very often from the other side of the house we hear a challenge to the effect that there is lack of cooperation. I know there is a system in Ottawa, one which is growing, concerning men who are seeking work on the railways, on the Rideau canal, or shovelling snow in front of public buildings. If a man wants to get work on the Rideau canal he has to go to the vice-chairman or the chairman of the Liberal-Conservative Association of the city of Ottawa, and there he is asked if he is a Liberal or a Conservative. I am positive of these facts. Before a man is put on the list so that he may obtain any kind of work from the government he has practically to sign a pledge and to pay the sum of one dollar before his name is entered on the list. He has to say he belongs to the Liberal-Conservative Association. I come from a section of the country where we do not believe in that system. I know that so far as the Cochrane district is concerned there is no playing of politics in regard to relief measures. I do not see any reason why in the city of Ottawa or anywhere in Canada such a system should be in existence. I know that patronage exists, and that it has existed in the past, but I have never heard of any man being asked to sign his allegiance to a certain party before he could get any work. Certainly that should not be done at the present time. Even the sum of one dollar means a lot to many of those men. Some of them would never receive any return from it. I know that if the country was aware of the situation, in view of

Supply-Public Works-Ontario
statements made by the government that there is no partisanship so far as the distribution of work is concerned, the government would be severely criticized. I protest against the practice I have described.

May I say in
reply that I know nothing of what happened in the Department of Railways and Canals. I do know that a few years ago when we were on the other side of the house and my friends were on this side of the house I heard similar charges made.
And will again.

So far as the
Department of Public Works is concerned I do not know of any such practice as he suggests exists. I do know however that from time to time I receive complaints that we are employing too many Liberals in connection with work of this kind.

May I say a word in reply to the hon. member, since he has attacked my department. I do not admit that any such condition exists as he has described, namely, that men have to pay a dollar before they can obtain a position. I admit frankly however, generally speaking, that so far as the appointment of workers on works of my department in the city of Ottawa or elsewhere is concerned, we very frequently do accept the recommendations of the Conservative committee. What is the use of implying anything else, because everybody knows, as the Minister of Public Works has pointed out, that the same charge was made from our side of the house against the last government?
I say quite honestly and quite sincerely that there is no difference, generally speaking, between the system which obtains under this government and that which obtained under the previous one. Not only that, but I believe generally speaking there is a good deal to be said in defence of the practice. I do not mean to suggest that when a man is destitute he should not be given consideration; many of them are. Irrespective of a committee in this city I have on a number of occasions given positions to men who, it was represented to me, where in destitute circumstances. That often occurs, I have not any doubt, in the Department of Public Works, my own department and in others. But, generally speaking, it is obvious that the government in power, whether it be Liberal, Conservative or even a government of my hon. friends in the corner-when, a thousand years from now, they gain power-* will probably do likewise. It will naturally give consideration to its friends. I do not
think any just criticism can be levelled at that. I do not admit however that the system is, in detail, as pointed out by the hon. member. When my estimates are up for consideration I shall be happy to discuss the whole matter.

I wish to repeat that there is a list of those belonging to the Liberal-Conservative Association of the city of Ottawa. The Minister of Railways has mentioned the fact that there is a partisan system. I do not agree with that principle, no matter what party is in power. We do not do that in our section of the country. There is this fact, however, that men whose names appear on the list have to pay one dollar. The Minister of Railways and Canals would not accuse the late government of adopting that practice.
I do not admit that it exists now, either.
I repeat the statement that it does exist.
That does not prove it.

I will give hundreds
of names, if necessary. If a man is to get any kind of work he has to pay a dollar and sell his soul to the Conservative party to get on that list. I say that that is not fair. The Minister of Railways and Canals would not accuse the late administration of having compelled men to pay the sum of one dollar to belong to the Liberal party and to get work.
That is exactly what they were accused of. Whether it was true or not, the fact is that that was the accusation.

That does not help the situation. We have been challenged by hon. members opposite to give cooperation. May I say we are willing to give it, but we do not want such practices as this, and particularly under present conditions. I have had men visit me in this city of Ottawa who have told me that every man who gets work around these buildings or on the Rideau canal must sign allegiance to the Conservative party. I repeat that that is not fair.

Just because someone has
made that statement to the hon. member does not necessarily prove that it is true. Frequently men state things which are not true or correct. However, I shall look into the whole matter, and shall gladly discuss it later.

I should like to thank the
Minister of Public Works for the manner in which he has responded to my request for

information concerning my constituency. However, may I inform him if he does not already know it, that no Liberal has had a job in the county of Bona venture since the Conservative party has been in office. I am not blaming him for that. In our parishes the party leaders have the spending of the money, and they employ their own friends. Probably they are following in the footsteps of the party who preceded them. I am pleased to note that our amiable and truthful friend, the Minister of Railways and Canals, has made a public acknowledgment to-day as to the system prevailing now. It would seem to be the system that to the victors belong the spoils.
Another circumstance comes to my mind at this time. 1 believe it was in 1929 that the then leader of the opposition, the Prime Minister of to-day, read a letter to this house from the county of Bonaventure complaining severely that the party affected was unable to obtain work because he was a Conservative. The leader of the opposition of that day, the right hon. .gentleman who sits opposite to-day, protested strongly at that time against the practice he described. He stated that poor labourers, no matter what their allegiance was, should be employed, irrespective of party. I should like to have that policy followed at the present time.
It is being followed.

In my constituency there are poor men who do not know where to turn for their meals. If they are to be punished because they voted for the Liberal party I must say that would not seem to be a very fair way of distributing public money. I would ask the minister in connection with any further works that he grants to my constituency to instruct the overseer to see that the work is divided equally. The parish priests have asked from the pulpit that those who are most in need should be given the work and that it should not be confined wholly to one party. That is the reason I am bringing the matter to the minister's attention and raising objection at this time.
I could show to my hon. friend a sheaf of letters from Conservative committees in his constituency complaining that the Liberals are still in power down there.

That is misinformation.
Mr. STEWART (Leeds) And that they are getting all the work and furnishing all the supplies.
Not in Bonaventure county.
And that the Conservatives are not getting a fair share of the work even when it is being done by day labour.
Misinformation.
I am telling you honestly the information I am getting.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased of the opportunity afforded to me of discussing patronage. The hon. member for Timiskaming North (Mr. Bra-dette) mentioned, just now, a kind of a pledge that people have to sign, in Ottawa. I hold in my hand such a pledge from a Liberal club of Quebec. These pledges are not solely required for work entirely paid by one or another government, but also for such work which is paid by both Dominion and provincial governments, in connection with unemployment relief. Instructions to show preference to members of this club are given to engineers of various districts, not only by political organizations but directly by the Quebec government. I have here a document addressed to a highway engineer, instructing him to employ, in relief work, for the repairs of a certain road, 75 per cent Liberals and 25 per cent Conservatives. The hon. member for Timiskaming should come and give a lecture, on the subject, to the Liberals of Quebec, but especially to the Prime Minister of that province.

Since I asked the question in regard to the Montreal armouries I have been advised by the departmental official that the specifications for the Toronto armouries do not stipulate that the material-I am not sure whether all the material or not-to be usedi in the construction of these armouries shall be of Canadian or at least of British manufacture. I am very grateful for the minister's statement a moment ago that so far as lies within his power he will see to it that the material going into these armouries will be Canadian, or at least British material. Construction on the armouries has not yet gone far enough for the use of material of general manufacture, and while the specifications it is said do not call for the material to be made in Canada, I trust that the minister will make every effort, as I know he will, to see that the material so far as possible is Canadian. He is just as anxious as I or any other member of the house that Canadian material and Canadian labour be used as far as possible in the construction of all buildings for dominion purposes. I do know that all the specifications issued for

Supply-Public Works-Ontario
buildings which the department itself erects specify that the material must be of Canadian or British manufacture,' and if it is not too late to take action in reference to these buildings that are being erected outside of departmental control, I hope that similar action will be taken. I have no criticism whatever of the specifications other than that.
I am told that they are excellent specifications, nor have I any criticism to offer of the contractors, who I am told are the very best, nor of the sub-contractors or workmen. May I suggest that the Finance minister raise the tariff in his next budget so that the request of my hon. friend (Mr. MacNicol), and not my desires, may be complied with?

I have no doubt that that would meet with the approval of my hon. friend who has just spoken. I thank the minister
very much for his remarks.

To ease the mind of my hon. friend from Toronto Northwest, may I remind him that the minister who controls importations into this country will see to it that an embargo is placed on the importation of outside goods. I think my hon. friend can rest his soul in peace because, according to the letters I am getting, there is no danger under this ministry of any goods getting into Canada, even from the British Empire, if Canadian goods are available. I cannot understand how anyone who favours tariffs, embargoes and restrictions to the extent my hon. friend does should be at all alarmed over the possibility of foreign material coming into competition with Canadian.
I am anxious for Canadian workmen to get as much work as possible.

A few days ago, in
reply to a question, the Minister of Public Works gave the amount that was being paid for rentals of buildings for the use of the government in this city. I have not the figures before me but they ran into hundreds of thousands of dollars. I understand, and I wish to be corrected if I am wrong, that two floors of the new Confederation building are unoccupied at the present time. If that is true, it would seem to the ordinary man that the whole of that new building should be occupied before further rentals are paid in the city of Ottawa.
I can assure my hon. friend that his information again is absolutely incorrect.
Why again?

There is no space in the Confederation building of any importance that is not occupied. There is not one floor nor half a floor that is not occupied. The amount of rentals paid in the city of Ottawa has been very substantially reduced, and we are now paying over $100,000 less than before we went into the Confederation building, and since we have given up some rentals that we had.

Referring to the question
that has been brought up by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bra-dette), and in view of the frank admission of the Minister of Railways that there is discrimination or, shall I say, patronage with regard to appointments, although I thought we had done away with that-
Not under your regime.

The Prime Minister in the 1930 session promised on his honour from the floor of this house that there would be no such thing as discrimination or patronage in connection with these public works that were being undertaken for purposes of relief. I hold in my hand P.'C. 2043, dated August 5, 1931. I feel sure the government believe in their own orders in council, and I should like to quote clause 9 of this one, which reads:
All agreements with provincial and municipal authorities shall contain a provision to the effect that all persons employed on the works or undertakings referred to herein shall be residents of Canada, and so far as practicable of the locality in which the work is being performed, and in no case shall discrimination be made or permitted in the employment of, or in the granting of direct relief to any British subjects by reason of their political affiliation, race or religious views.
I think that is a very good principle.

May I interrupt the hon.
gentleman? We were not discussing direct relief, and I do not think the discussion of that matter is in order. The hon. member for Timiskaming referred to ordinary work on the canal.
I wish the minister would let me finish.
I consider the hon. gentleman as being out of order in discussing direct relief on an estimate of the Minister of Public Works.
If the minister heard the order in council which was read, he would realize that it referred not only to direct relief but to employment.

I was not talking about
the order in council, I was talking about the discussion. The hon. gentleman has no need to tell me what I am talking about.

The Minister of Railways seems to be very glib. He rose to a point of order and I am only suggesting that the hon. gentleman was talking about an order in council which deals not only with direct relief but with employment. Reference to such an order in council is in order during the discussion of public works estimates.

I like to be called to
order once in a while by the Minister of Railways even though he may not be the chairman of the assembly. If the government insists upon such a principle in the case of the provinces and the municipalities, it should be good enough for them to carry out themselves. I think it is a shame and a disgrace to see a member of the government stand up and tell this house during times like this when there is so much distress through the country that they are actually taking recommendations of Conservative associations as to who is to receive employment. I agree that in normal times there might be something to be said about such a practice but this government is supposed to enforce this principle in connection with the provinces and the municipalities and yet they act at variance with it, as has been admitted by the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works.

I did not admit discrimination at all. I took the attitude that in the case of ordinary work on the canals- nothing to do with relief work-this government was doing the same as the last government. I am not hypocrite enough to say

that, generally speaking, we do not prefer our friends to our enemies. As far as I am concerned personally, I would prefer a friend to an enemy where there is work to be performed. As far as relief work is concerned, so far as I know nothing in the shape of patronage has been practised. If I understood the order in council correctly, it deals entirely with relief matters and has no connection with ordinary work on the canals. As I have pointed out on many occasions, I have appointed people to ordinary canal work who had nothing to do with committees but I shall be quite frank and admit that, generally speaking, when ordinary work on the ' canals is let we do exactly the same as the late government did when they were in power. As a general rule, we take the recommendations of our friends.
Does the minister mean his past enemies or his present enemies?
The hon. member will find out.

The order in council quoted by the hon. member for Kenora (Mr, Heenan) is in connection with expenditures specifically earmarked for the relief of unemployment. This department issued instructions to all its district engineers and architects that under no circumstances should there be any discrimination and that wherever possible they should consult the mayor, the reeve or the head of the municipality and make a fair distribution of the employment. I do not intend to ask for the amounts spent in the various provinces by his department, but if he will go back as far as confederation I know he will find that the amounts spent in the three western provinces do not begin to compare with what has been spent in other provinces.
We do need public buildings in many places but I like the suggestion made by the minister that certain towns might put up community halls in which could be provided suitable space for a post office- I again offer the same suggestion that I made two years ago that in -many places the federal and provincial governments should cooperate in the erection of public buildings. Such a building could house the telephone office and post office, and perhaps one or two other government offices. The building could be taken care of by one janitor, it would be cheaper for everybody and would provide better accommodation for the public. There are some places where this could be done, and I think in this respect there should be cooperation between the federal and provincial governments.
I hope the minister presses his suggestion in connection with the erection of community halls in the smaller places. There are many places which need such accommodation. In my own constituency I believe there is only one public building, but I speak subject to correction. I have received requests from three towns for post office buildings, and they are needed badly in each case. I am putting

these facts forward in order that the minister can assure the government that there is a real need for the construction of public buildings in various places in Canada. I am sure that nearly every hon. member could tell the minister of places where a public building is needed. I shall be glad to furnish him with a list of the places in my constituency. I remember asking a former minister of public works how much he could spend if a public building was erected in every place where the citizens had asked for it, and he replied that while he had not made an estimate, he thought he could spend well over $100,000,000.
You would have to inflate the currency.

That would not be a very dangerous inflation, seeing that we have been deflated in currency and credit to the extent of about $700,000,000. Without saying anything more, I urge the minister to present to the other members of the cabinet the requests for public buildings which I am sure he has filed in his office. I take it for granted that most of these requests are warranted.

I should like to direct the minister's attention to a number of very modest projects which are needed in my province. Most of these are known already to him, either by letter or by personal interview. I should like to gather them up together and put them before him at this time, as most of them come within the terms of the blanket vote for "harbours and rivers generally, for maintenance of services, no new works to be undertaken." These facilities are urgently needed in connection with the fishing industry, particularly the activities of the shore fishermen. They are needed for the
purpose of providing safe landing for boats, protection and shelter, and for convenience. That is to say, with the proper facilities the men would not need to leave on the tide an hour or two earlier than they must do at present. With a proper wharf or breakwater the men would be able to have their boats afloat and leave at a later hour. I might say to the minister that these men leave at three, four and five o'clock in the morning and if there are no facilities, they have to return on the tide. Sometimes this return is under pretty strenuous conditions when rough weather happens to kick up while they are out.
The first project is the completion of some work already undertaken at West Baccaro. There was a breakwater and boat harbour there which served this community which is down on the most southerly and westerly point of Nova Scotia at Cape Sable. The activities of this community are confined almost exclusively to fishing, both lobster and) fresh. A boat harbour and breakwater is essential and these facilities have been destroyed or injured by storms. I believe the minister has a report in connection with this matter, as some work has been done already.
The total amount needed to complete the projects I have in mind would not amount to a quarter of what we have just voted for military buildings. The vote for military buildings totals about $100,000. There are items which cannot be deleted because they are under contract, but the people do not understand why these large amounts shouldi be voted for such projects when they cannot get the modest sum needed to provide them with very necessary facilities.
The next item is the extension to the breakwater at the west endi of upper Surette island. This is another fishing community, and a breakwater would be of great service to the people. The next is repairs to the public wharf and extension of the breakwater at Shag Harbour. When we speak of breakwaters we generally think of them as being large projects, but the one needed at Shag Harbour would be a modest affair and could be carried out with the expenditure of comparatively few dollars. A little dredging is needed at The Hawk and this could be done with departmental dredge, number sixteen. This community is located on Cape Sable island out near Clarke's Harbour, well out in the Atlantic, and the protection is needed for the fishermen. A breakwater was built at Louishead in 1887 but it has been practically demolished. This is a fishing community and the destruction of that facility has proven
664	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.S.
to be a very serious matter to the people. Some work has been done at Lower East Pubnico, and I should like the minister to carry it on and provide the necessary facilities for this community. The fishermen now find it necessary to go a long distance to the fishing grounds and this facility would prove of great help. Another matter is the building of a road between the landing and the light on Bon Portage island. This would require an expenditure of only a few hundred dollars.
These requests are very modest but they are in the interests of the fishermen. They are needed for the carrying on of their activities and the expenditure of this money would assist in providing employment. It would not be in the nature of direct relief, because it would provide a facility which is as nearly self-liquidating as anything could be; that is to say, it would assist people in carrying on their ordinary vocations. I do urge on the minister favourable consideration of these matters, either in connection with this vote or in connection with whatever program of public works for relief may be carried on. These are not relief projects the utility of which is questionable; they will provide a useful addition to the equipment of these people for carrying on their work.
There are three more or less major projects and these have to came within the relief vote, or at least a supplementary estimate for public works. First there is the need of a facility at Lockeport, the money for which was voted some three or four years ago. The contract was let, but that was cancelled after this government came in. That money was intended for the provision of some sort of suitable facility in Lockeport harbour to afford protection for boats as well as protection for the shore owing to the situation there due to the action of the sea. The fishermen down there have got together in reference to this facility and have determined that this is what would be best-(because there has been a good deal of confusion and difference of opinion. The practically unanimous decision is for some sort of substantial piece of blocking, not necessarily attached to the shore, which would probably be the most suitable facility for protecting the boats there.
Another needed improvement is a wharf at Yarmouth, with regard to which representations have recently been made to the Minister of Finance and probably direct to the minister as well. That is a major work. Yarmouth is an important port. There is no public wharf there, but there are a number of private wharves, and the provision of a public wharf would afford employment to men there and 
would encourage a thriving port which does a great deal of business. It would be to the advantage not only of that section of the country as well as of the whole province of Nova Scotia, but of the country at large, because it is essentially a Canadian, port. There are more passengers in and out that port throughout the year than in any other port in Canada. Hon. members may be surprised at that, but owing to the Boston and New York services you will find that the passenger service there is greater throughout the year than in any other Canadian port including Montreal, Halifax and Vancouver.
The other major item is the completion of a breakwater at Port Maitland, a facility which has been needed by the fishermen and the provision of which, so far as it has been constructed, has been of great benefit, having practically provided a harbour where otherwise there would have been open shore, and where a very large fishing industry is prosecuted, both in fresh fish and in lobster.
I commend these three items to the minister, not in connection with this particular vote but in connection with a supplementary vote or in connection with any program which may be instituted by this government in the way of public works for relief purposes.

As I recall,
nearly all these items have been the subject of correspondence and representation in the recent past. It will be seen that the vote has been reduced from last year and it covers the whole of the province. We shall have to take into consideration the demands and requirements of other sections and try to harmonize them, doing the best we can. I am glad that the hon. gentleman has collected them all together and summarized the situation, and I shall give consideration to the larger projects in connection with any program of public works that may be determined.

The small ones are
needed as much as the large items, but I thought they might be taken care of in connection with the general item.
It is no exaggeration to say that there are hundreds of similar requests, and we shall have to do the best we can for all sections.
Where is Lunenburg?

I say to my hon. friend he
does not know his geography. The government have put in the estimates only $4,500 for the whole county of Lunenburg, one of the greatest fishing areas not only in Nova Scotia but in the Dominion of Canada. All that the government, on account of mismanagement, on account of the fact that they are strangling trade and not trying to do anything for the Canadian people, can put in the estimates for that great county is $4,500. The same policy applies to everything else. I notice in the item of harbours and rivers generally, a reduction of $50,000. Last year the item was $275,000; the year before, if I remember correctly, it was $325,000; in 1930 it was $400,000. I am sorry my good friend the Minister of Finance is not present. He at least should have got something for his county in Nova Scotia, but in the estimates there is not one
666	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.S.
dollar for the constituency represented by him. This government is riding for a fall as far as Nova Scotia is concerned. I am sorry for my Conservative friends opposite; they should have some influence with the government because they are all strong, silent men, especially silent; but they sit quietly in their seats and allow the Minister of Public Works and the government to bring down these estimates, only five out of twenty counties in Nova Scotia being given a single dollar to try to encourage the fishermen and other businessmen of that great province. This is a shame and a crime. Of course it may be possible that my friend the junior member for Halifax, the hon. member for Pietou, the hon. member for Cumberland, the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the others are being lulled to sleep by the Minister of Public Works or the Prime Minister because perhaps they have been promised part of this $50,000,000 which it is rumoured is to be voted- for public works. Why not come out into the open? If we are going to vote that large amount, a portion of which Nova Scotia must get, why not put the items in the estimates?
As far as my county is concerned, politically the less money the government insert in the estimates, the better I like it, because every knock is a boost; every dollar they do not appropriate, means that I shall get more votes in that constituency and I thank the Minister of Public Works and the government for not spending a dollar there, because in the last fortnight I have been receiving letters from Tories as well as Grits saying that when the next election takes place they will give me a greater majority than ever before.

There is just
one interpretation that I can place upon the remarks of the hon. gentleman: I am forced to the conclusion that his appreciation of the people of Nova Scotia is that they vote according to the amount of money spent in their constituencies.
Is the hon. member for Pietou going to stand for that?

I do not think that is a fair representation of the intelligence, the patriotism, of the people of Nova Scotia; it is a reflection upon them which they will resent very keenly when they come to cast their votes. Further, has my hon. friend not heard from his own side of the house a demand for economy throughout the country, for balanced budgets? He would disregard all that and say that this is the time when we should go out with open hands and spend money in the high, wide and handsome 
way in which his friends spent it, which expenditures unfortunately have seriously curtailed the revenues that are at the disposal of the government at this time. We are forced because of some of the reckless extravagances of the hon. gentleman's friends-
Oh, oh!
It is so.
The hon. member's party spent more than we did.

My hon. friend
knows quite well and no member knows better than he does the expenditures in connection with the Canadian National Railways have seriously handicapped the present government.

The hon. member agreed
to them.
No.

He accepted every one of
them.

Those expenditures made a serious inroad upon the revenues of this country, and as my hon. friend knows, these expenditures on public works are paid out of revenue and not from borrowings. If we accepted his contention, the budget instead of approaching balancing would be very much more in deficit than it is. Surely he does not consider a policy of that kind in these times of general depression is sound or one that any sane government would adopt.

When the committee rose at six o'clock the minister had just stated, if I understood him correctly, that the reason this small amount was placed in the main estimates for the province of Nova Scotia was that this money had to come out of revenue, and that he had to economize because the affairs of this country were in such bad shape when the government took office. I will admit that I am getting old, Mr. Chairman, and that I am old-fashioned ; I am willing to admit that my memory is bad, but I do not ask you to take my word. If you look at the votes and proceedings or Hansard or the public accounts for 1929 and 1930 you will see that when the budget was brought down in 1930 the Liberal government had a surplus over expenditures of some $82,000,000. So I do not see why to-day, after this government has been in power for four years and my hon. friend has been Minister of Public Works for that length of time, he should say that they can only spend this small sum of money in the great province of Nova 'Scotia because of the condition of affairs when they took office. Let me remind the minister that Nova Scotia is one of the maritime provinces, a province whose men go down to the sea in ships and do business in the great waters. The expenditure in that province has been reduced year by year so that now it is dowm to a minimum, and the minister says the reason is the policy of the government previous to 1930.
The minister was not satisfied with that; he had to drag in the railway question. He stated that the fact that the Liberal government had spent money on the railways of this country was another reason why he had to economize in his expenditures on public works. W ell, sir, I do not want to go outside of the items under consideration, but the expenditure on railways had or has nothing to do with the expenditure on harbours and rivers. We all know, however, that when the Liberal party took charge of this country we had only two streaks of rust from Vancouver to Halifax, and that by their policy the Liberal party built up a railway in this
country. In 1921 the deficit on the railways amounted to $90,000,000, butt when the Liberal party went out of office the railways wrnre practically paying their own way. With a Conservative majority in the Senate and a Liberal majority in this parliament we could ask for the construction of the Sunnybrae-Guys-borough branch line. Therefore I say that the minister should not try to camouflage the fact that so Htitle money is spent either in the province of Nova Scotia or elsewhere, because the same condition applies in every province. Why should the minister drag in the railway question or the fact that these amounts of money must be spent out of revenue?
I do not want to go into details, Mr. Chairman, but the minister should not pretend that this bluebook sets out all the money that is to be voted for public works; the Minister of Public Works knows the details better than I do, and he knows that in the last three or four years tens and hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent on public works by way of relief. I have no hesitation in saying that, so far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, in a large measure that money was wasted and never reached the people who should have received that so-called relief.
Before six o'clock my hon. friend tried to make out that this vote is small because the revenue is small. Who is to blame because the revenue is not greater? That is entirely due to the policies of this government. My hon. friend knows that in 1928, 1929 and 1930 the revenues of this country were expanding; he knows that in 1930 we had a surplus of $82,000,000, as I said before. The minister knows that trade has decreased under this government by at least seventy-five per cent. My hon. friend and his associates have so restricted Canada's trade that I cannot blame him for reducing expenditures. I pity him.
I pity members of the government because they have not seen the necessity for expanding our trade but instead, in order to satisfy certain interests within their own ranks, have endeavoured to restrict trade. As a result trade has dropped, and instead of having a total trade of over two billion dollars as under the Liberal government we have the condition with which we are only too familiar, both in regard to our trade with Great Britain and our trade with foreign countries. That is the reason the minister has to go to the council and to the treasury board and receive this little pittance for his department. I want to say to my hon. friends opposite that so far as the public works of this country are concerned, and so far as the maritime provinces, those great provinces of New Brunswick,

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.S.
Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are concerned, we bring new money into this country every year. We go down to the sea and every dollar that we bring in from it is new money which is spent in this country, money which we derive from foreign countries-money for the produce which we take from the sea and export. I want to say to my hon. friends opposite that to-day we have a situation in Nova Scotia due mostly to the actions and policies of this government whereby we are so constricted and handicapped that the people of the province of Nova Scotia, in the fishing section of this country, are practically starving. Again I appeal to the hon. member for Pictou, again to the hon. members for Halifax, and to the hon. member for Cape Breton North-Victoria who will no doubt agree with me that the greatest fishing area in his native province borders his own constituency. I appeal to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis and to every other hon. member from the province of Nova Scotia, and I say to them, "unite." I say that because I have no influence with this government-I do not want to have. Unite among yourselves and show the government that there is a great opportunity in the province of Nova Scotia, that there is connected with that province the greatest natural resource of this country-the fishing industry. How are hon. members going to improve the conditions when they vote- well, how much do they vote for my hon. friend's constituency? How much do they vote? Let me see, now-not a dollar for Annapolis-Digby, not a dollar for Cape Breton North-Victoria-not a dollar in the estimates. There is nothing in the estimates for Cumberland.

I had not expected to delay the passage of the minister's estimates, but because of the vociferous and stormy denunciation of the government we heard shortly before rising at six o'clock I think that in the interest of accuracy it would not be amiss for me to say a few words with special reference to the county I have the honour to represent in this house. I should not want the house to interpret my remarks to mean that I am perfectly satisfied that everything has been done that should be done with respect to public expenditures in the county of Cumberland or in the province of Nova Scotia. Furthermore I unhesitatingly say we anticipate that other expenditures will be made, perhaps in the very near future, which will more than make up for any delinquency there may be in the vote now before the committee.
In less than two years after this government took office upwards of 8100,000 was expended on public works in the county of Cumberland. The money was spent on wharves, harbours, harbour improvements, breakwaters, public buildings and other public services. In a period of less than three years that expenditure has amounted to upwards of $130,000. If the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough reads the papers I feel sure he will have observed that within the last ten days, through governmental action there has been given to one of the industries in the town of Amherst, which is in the county of Cumberland, a contract for upwards of half a million dollars. That money will be expended to the benefit of the town and tlhe people living therein, and will in a measure help to relieve the unemployment problem with which we are faced. Another firm in the constituency of Pictou has been given a contract of upwards of half a million dollars as well. I have not all the figures before me concerning expenditures in the province of Nova Scotia, but I have figures for one or two counties where expenditures have been made since July, 1930. I find that in the constituency of Digby-Annapolis over $600,000 has been expended. In order to be fair to the committee I should say that $250,000 or $300,000 of that was voted before the change of government. In the county of Halifax approximately one half million dollars has been expended. As I say, I have not had time to secure the amounts for the other counties in Nova Scotia, but I do assert that in the main the expenditures by this government since August of 1930 have been just as great relatively speaking as those made in the past by any government in Ottawa. I do not think that we have any
reason whatever to complain of the treatment accorded by this government. I should like to repeat before I sit down, as I said at the beginning, that I do not wish my remarks to be interpreted to mean that we are completely satisfied with everything, and that we feel that everything has been secured which we need. Far from that, but I do say that under the stress of world conditions the government has dealt fairly with us, so far as the expenditure of public money in the province of Nova Scotia is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I should like my deep-water friend, the commodore of the Lunenburg fleet, who with the full consent of all the great powers still maintains his position as Lord High Admiral of the LaHave, Georges and Grand Banks, to know how fully I appreciate his self-sacrificing, disinterested and forceful expression of interest in my constituency. The member for An-tigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) was most flattering in his references to my native county-all in good taste, and all within the strict bounds of truth. My gallant friend, however, in his zeal to berate the government, forgot for the moment that later we shall have supplementary estimates before us; also that old adage that all things come to those who wait. But may I also remind my hon. friend that if he will refer to the full list of public works in the county of Pictou receiving assistance at this time and be content to await the incoming supplementary tide he may perhaps then see that the county of Pictou is still floating in high water. If his constituency be not then equally fortunate I can assure him that he will have as sincere, if less vigorous an expression of my sympathy. That is all I can do for him under the circumstances.

So far as the county of Cape Breton North-Victoria which I have the honour to represent is concerned, while we have not got just what we would like, I must say that during the last year the Public Works department have spent over $150,000 in developing the natural resources in my constituency. They have developed there a gypsum mine which has been one of the most important events in the history of the county, and all this has been done in the last two years. Before that, for many years we had been trying in vain to get a breakwater built. Within the last two years this government has spent over $125,000 on the breakwater alone. The development of the gypsum mine I spoke of is a great contribution to the solution of the problem of unemployment. The solution of that problem lies in the creation of new
670	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.S.
industries to provide work, and at this mine at Dingwall there is now employed a great number of men, and the mine is shipping gypsum not only to Canada, but, as the president, Mr. MacFarlane, informed me only yesterday, to England, where it has never been shipped before. The mine has a contract for five thousand tons of gypsum to be shipped to England, and all this is due to this government having spent money at Dingwall and opening up this great industry, building the breakwater, and dredging the harbour so that vessels could come in. Never before had a vessel entered that harbour, but last year before navigation closed, two thousand tons of gypsum were shipped out of Dingwall harbour across the Atlantic to England. So this government has done something for my county and for the development of our natural resources.

I am delighted, Mr. Chairman, that I have got my hon. friends from Pictou (Mr. Cantley), Cumberland (Mr. Smith) and Cape Breton North-Victoria (Mr. Johnstone) to speak, and now that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has come into the house he may have a few remarks to make after I am through. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of course not.

I am somewhat surprised at that, and I am more surprised that the hon. gentlemen now sitting as members of the government did not take that position when they sat in opposition. I remember quite distinctly that in 1927 when I was asked for a report connected with certain post office trouble in the city of Saint John I then stated that reports had come from our inspectors, and that I considered them confidential. I was forced to produce them on the table of the house. I remember quite distinctly that I agreed that the leader of the opposition of that day, the present Prime Minister, should name a committee of five to whom I would submit all the reports, for their information. The reports were submitted for such information. Then, after the committee had finished its work the then leader of the opposition took the re-

ports and read them into Hansard from the floor of this house. If on that occasion it was right for them to be submitted to the house, or to be put on the table, why is it not proper procedure now?
I think there is a clear distinction between the two cases.
There is no distinction at all; they are both confidential reports.

In the case to which the hon. member has referred there was a charge against a certain official, and the reports were in connection with that incident. The reports now in question are made for the purpose of enabling the minister and the department to decide on a certain line of action.
And the reports to which I referred were made to enable the Postmaster General to decide upon a certain line of action.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No; one was a matter of policy and the other was not.

These reports are on the file of the Department of Public Works and are not on the minister's confidential file. There is no official in the department, other than the minister, who has a confidential file. These are public documents, documents which the people of this country pay to have made up. W e have to pay money to send these engineers around to the different parts of the provinces to find out w'hat works are necessary, and they submit those recommendations to the minister. I say they are not confidential, and that this House of Commons ought to have the right to see what works were recommended by the officials who are paid by this country, and to see what works were cut out either by the government or by the treasury officials.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The comment came later. But there is a distinction between the two sets of circumstances. As the hon. gentleman will realize, having been Postmaster General, and as the former Minister of the Interior and the former Minister of Agriculture will understand, when the time comes to prepare estimates it has been the custom ever since there has been responsible government to send out people who make reports, and the government adopts its policy. It then determines what action shall be taken, and assumes the whole responsibility. If it were otherwise the hon. member for Antagonish-Guysborough will understand the result would be that the officials would be the responsible parties, and not the ministers who bring them to this House of Commons. Their recommendations would be the basis of discussion in parliament, and not the estimates at all. That is my understanding, and I have no desire to suggest that a course different from that which has been followed should be followed in the present instance. However, that has been my understanding of it since I have known about parliamentary institutions; for if at the present moment we were to substitute a recommendation of engineers or others for the responsibility accepted by the administration we would have an entirely different system of government. I recall now what the hon. gentleman mentions. It was in connection with Griffiths, and there was a man called Woods. I recall it quite well now. But if my hon. friend looks at it, he will see that that is entirely a different thing.

If I may be permitted,
Mr. Chairman, I cannot agree with the Prime Minister in the matter of confidential information. I can well understand that when an engineer makes a report to a minister on a certain public work, and gives an estimate on the price, his estimates should be confidential until the contract is awarded.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, up to that point.

My hon. friend is quite correct in assuming that attitude. But when an engineer makes a report asked for by the minister on the necessity of certain public works in a province, his report should not be confidential.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Why not?

Why should it be? That is not establishing the policy of the government. If it were establishing the policy of the government I would say yes, it should be confidential. But the policy of the government is to carry on public works in this country to a greater or certain extent, and the details of that policy are not confidential once you begin to work out the policy. Then parliament is entitled to the information, except that when contracts have to be let based on an estimate of the engineer, then in fairness to the people who are tendering, in fairness to the contractor and the engineer, the estimate should be confidential.
I go a step further. Time and again I have asked for papers and reports of engineers in connection with public works by way of motion, and I have got them; but I took very good care not to ask for them until after the tenders had been awarded, because up to that point I felt they were confidential. After the contract is awarded, however, they are no longer confidential.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
