I do not rise to criticize this vote, although it is very meagre. The government has explained that it is unable to spend more money this year because of the depression, and I do not want to add anything to what has been said tonight with respect to the depression. If the government's policies were changed I do not think there would be any necessity for such drastic cuts in necessary public service. However, I have another object in view in speaking this evening. Every once in a while someone from eastern Canada takes it upon himself to point out the tremendous costs incurred by the government in western Canada. I ask my hon. friends from eastern Canada to glance through the proposed expenditures for the three prairie provinces. The estimates this year are no different from those of the past thirteen years. I am not so familiar with conditions before that time, but the country was new and the expenditures could not have been heavy. No individual in eastern Canada has the right to say, either publicly or privately, that the government of Canada is making huge expenditures in western Canada. With the single exception of the expenditures for relief, a calamity similar to occurrences in the past in the east, it would be hard to discover expenditures of any great amount. Time and again we are treated to a tirade by people in eastern Canada to the effect that the cost of carrying western Canada is out of all proportion to the cost applicable to the rest of the country. I want to state publicly that for the past thirteen years the 2,000,000 people who live in the western provinces have not had anything like their fair share of expenditure. To-night we have listened to the complaints of hon. gentlemen from the old province of Nova Scotia sitting on both sides of the house. Year after year the eastern provinces have been voted ten times the amount voted to the three prairie provinces. The cost to the federal government of carrying the western provinces has been small compared with the expenditures made in other parts of the country. I exclude British Columbia because 
that province has a coast line and at times heavy expenditures have been made in that connection. Some of these complaints come from the maritime provinces-I do not say they are made by hon. members of this house, but they are made by very influential people. They do not go down very well with us in the west, particularly with those of us who happen to have been acquainted with the estimates for years past and are likely to see them in the future, because we have no rivers, no dredging, no harbours, so that all we get from the federal government-and we are taxpayers equally with the people in the east- is money for repairs to public buildings and once in a while a public building. I can quite imagine that my hon. friend from East Edmonton has made representations. I know that there is necessity for expenditures in the west as well as in the north which is opening up, but we shall not get them; I find in the estimates no appropriations for work of that sort. I rise now to protest against that kind of thing. In the light of these estimates, and of the estimates of previous years, I say that the residents of western Canada have not received anything like their proportionate share of the expenditures voted year by year by the federal government. If you glance at the estimates this year you see that the expenditure is so paltry as hardly to be worth mentioning. I know that representations have been made to the Department of Public Works and to other departments as well for expenditures; but we are told-rather, I1 should say, they are told, because I am not now in the habit of inquiring-that the money cannot be given; the depression is on, and therefore it cannot be done. I venture to say however that when this government changes, as it will change when there is a general election, the depression will not cut much of a figure in the demands that will be made upon the successors of hon. gentlemen now in the government. We shall hear in no uncertain way, when the Liberal government is in office, that money ought to be spent.
I have not a great deal of sympathy with my hon. friend who is getting such a panning to-night, because in former days he was one of the gentlemen who contributed their fair share of the panning of ministers in the previous government. He knows now what the responsibilities are like and he must be prepared for a pretty severe castigation, not only on his own account but for the sins of his fellow members in the government. He and some of his friends were fairly good at criticizing in more prosperous days, and I would submit to him now that the prosperity then

What a wonderful country Canada was going to be; what a wonderful place to live in. But now we hear excuses made on any and every occasion that there is a world depression. There was no world depression in 1930, however; hon. gentlemen never heard of such a thing. All the fault then was the government's. My hon. friends cannot change their argument.
I am amazed as I sit here and watch the performance of hon. gentlemen opposite that in very few particulars have they changed the method of administration in any respect. They are carrying on very much in the way the government whom they succeeded carried on, and day by day they are finding out that after all the old government was not such a poor government, that its methods were not so terribly bad as my hon. friends opposite depicted them. When it comes to administration they have to carry on very much in the same way. They were going to nationalize unemployment, but they have to carry on through the agency of the provincial governments. My hon. friend is spending some money-very little, and it is being reduced- but another agency will spend it and do some of the work formerly performed by the Minister of Public Works.
Taking it all in all, therefore, there is a tremendous difference between sitting on this side and sitting on that side. I must confess that there is great freedom from anxiety over here. There is one gentleman with whom once in a while I do sympathize, and I say that freely, and that is the Minister of Finance. He is the one who has to find the money, and I say to my hon. friends opposite that their policies make it absolutely impossible for him to find it. Year by year he is finding himself in this difficulty, a difficulty every year aggravated. Every year there is a little more cut off expenditures-why? Because we cannot get the revenue, and if there were no election in sight for the next two years this performance would go on, with constantly decreasing revenues. No reference is made to the fact that we are losing over S100,000,000 in customs and excise, though the Minister of Finance knows it. But that is to be made up by direct taxation from some other source. Notwithstanding all the additional taxation, however, we have to admit, when we glance through the estimates, that they are going down, with the result that very much needed services will have to remain in abeyance.
I want to make it perfectly clear that I am ready to take up the cudgels on behalf of my own part of the province, and I say with full assurance that not only are we not getting more than we are entitled to, but we are not getting our fair share. Perhaps I must take my share of the responsibility as well as anyone else, but the fact remains that every western member should take up the cudgels on this question, because it is so irritating at times when we read in the press, or hear, such statements as have been made. I do know that the gentleman who made the statement when he came to Ottawa took it back. I have no desire to raise any question about east versus west, but statements of that kind are not true.

I need not tell the committee that of all the provinces of Canada perhaps Prince Edward Island has a coast line which involves the greatest number of public works, but these have been allowed to fall into decay very rapidly in the past few years. As the hon. member for Antigon-ish-Guysborough said, we need assistance for

our fishermen, and the only assistance we can give is to provide them with facilities in the way of harbours and landings.
There is one matter to which I would like to direct the attention of the committee. The estimates presented by my good friend the Minister of Finance the second day of the session are no more the estimates for this dominion than that telephone directory is out in the lobby. We have had the information, perhaps by way of accident, from a good many hon. gentlemen opposite as to what is the situation. We know that two or three months before the session opened there were demands from every city and town across the country asking this government to cut down on expenditures, and when the estimates were tabled great headlines appeared in the press from coast to coast saying the estimates hadi been reduced by 817,000,000. But our friends from Nova Scotia say: "Wait until the supplementary estimates are brought down; then wc will be floating on top of the ocean." They say these do not begin to be the estimates for 1934.
I want to point out that the Minister of Finance has not played fair with the country. If we are to have supplementary estimates that will wipe out the S17,000,000 which he said he was saving, it is absolutely unfair to the people of Canada. I think the estimates should have contained every item of expenditure contemplated by the government so that each item could be brought down in the house and passed in the regular way. We do not know how this tremendous amount of new money is to be expended. Some say it is to be a blank cheque; some say it is to be expended under the peace, order and good government legislation, while some say it will be in the supplementary estimates. At all events there is nothing in the estimates for the county I represent, and very little for the counties represented by my hon. friends opposite.
The question I want to ask the minister is whether any representations have been made to him with regard to the warehouses on the wharf at Summerside, Prince Edward Island, and whether a request has been made for the construction of a heated warehouse at that point for the handling of potatoes and other products.

I think some
representations were made in connection with the government taking over the Canadian National Railways warehouse. As to the amount in the estimates for Prince Ediward

Island, of course it is small but I think my hon. friend will find that it is only in keeping with the estimates for the other provinces.. With regard to his fears as to the supplementary estimates and further expenditures,. I can only invite him to be patient and wait and see. If any action is taken along: that line, he will have an opportunity, as all others will have, to set forth his views and express his claims. We have always had supplementary estimates since I have been in this house, and there may be some this-year; I cannot say.
Mr. MaicLEAN:	A portion of that wharf
has been taken over and maintained by your department, but on that wharf we have a couple of potato warehouses. This year, however, a great deal of trouble was experienced in loading and housing the' potatoes in those buildings, because of frost. A request has been made by the board of trade and other organizations of Summerside asking that some improvements be made there in order that these buildings might be heated so that potatoes could be shipped in colder weather than is possible at present. I hope that if there are supplementary estimates, as we have been led to believe, a sufficient amount will be included to take care of these very necessary repairs.
There are other repairs all around the county that I could enumerate by the score; I could point out many places where money should have been expended this year, and I hope that when the supplementary estimates are brought down these very much needed repairs will not be overlooked.
